timed_text.text: day 21. When you face a challenge, a big competition, a moment of adversity, something that
tests you, your brain does something automatic. It imagines the worst case, embarrassment, failure,
loss, that fear scenario. That's not weakness. That's your nervous system doing exactly
what it was designed to do. That threat response is ancient. It was built to keep you
alive. And it still fires the same way whether you're facing a predator or stepping on
the starting line. There are two types of athletes in those moments. The victim and the fighter.
The victim acknowledges the fear and becomes it. They make excuses. They shrink. They find
reasons why the situation is unfair or why they're not ready. And they stay on the safe side of
the line. The fighter acknowledges the same fear and steps over the line anyway. Because
they're not afraid because they decided the fear doesn't get to make the call. The difference isn't
talent. It isn't physical preparation. It's a decision made in the seconds before the whistle
blows about who gets to be in charge. You or the fear. You've been building the tools to make
that decision automatically. Today we name it explicitly on your screen to go into identify
your line and declare which side you choose.

cards.prompt: Describe the fear you feel before your most challenging competitive moments. Be specific — what does it say? What worst-case scenario does your brain go to?
Now name it for what it is — your brain trying to protect you. It's not the truth. It's a signal.
The fighter steps over the line anyway. What does stepping over the line look like for you — specifically, in the moment that fear arrives?
